claim: Zbtb20 is a member of the bric-a-brac tramtrack broad complex/poxvirus and zinc domain family.
source: ZBTB20 is a member of the bric-a-brac tramtrack broad complex/poxvirus and zinc domain family, which functions primarily as transcriptional factors via interactions mediated by their conserved C2H2 Krüppel-type zinc finger and BTB/POZ domains (Mitchelmore et al., 2002; Zhang et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Mitchelmore et al., 2002; Zhang et al., 2001).

claim: ZBTB20 functions primarily as a transcriptional factor via interactions mediated by conserved C2H2 Krüppel-type zinc finger and BTB/POZ domains.
source: ZBTB20 is a member of the bric-a-brac tramtrack broad complex/poxvirus and zinc domain family, which functions primarily as transcriptional factors via interactions mediated by their conserved C2H2 Krüppel-type zinc finger and BTB/POZ domains (Mitchelmore et al., 2002; Zhang et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Mitchelmore et al., 2002; Zhang et al., 2001).

claim: ZBTB20 is involved in metabolism, development, growth, glucose homeostasis, and immune responses.
source: Previous studies have indicated that ZBTB20 could be involved in metabolism, development, growth, glucose homeostasis, and immune responses (Liu et al., 2013; Ren et al., 2014; Sutherland et al., 2009; Xie et al., 2010, 2008; Zhang et al., 2015, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies (Liu et al., 2013; Ren et al., 2014; Sutherland et al., 2009; Xie et al., 2010, 2008; Zhang et al., 2015, 2012).

claim: Missense mutations of ZBTB20 have been linked to Primrose syndrome.
source: More importantly, missense mutations of ZBTB20 have been linked to Primrose syndrome (Cordeddu et al., 2014), suggesting that transcription factor ZBTB20 is an essential element for neurological disorders.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study (Cordeddu et al., 2014).

claim: Mice lacking Zbtb20 exhibited impaired evening activity rhythms both in 12-hr light/12-hr dark (LD) cycles and under constant darkness conditions (DD).
source: Here, we found that mice lacking Zbtb20 exhibited impaired evening activity rhythms both in 12-hr light/12-hr dark (LD) cycles and under constant darkness conditions (DD).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Zbtb20 mRNA was reduced by 90% in the SCN of NS-ZB20KO mice.
source: In the NS-ZB20KO mice, the amount of Zbtb20 estimated by quantitative RT-PCR (Q-PCR) was reduced by 90% in the SCN, 70% in the olfactory bulb and 90% in the cerebellum in NS-ZB20KO mice, with no change observed in Zbtb20 expression in the liver (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by Q-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Zbtb20 mRNA was reduced by 70% in the olfactory bulb of NS-ZB20KO mice.
source: In the NS-ZB20KO mice, the amount of Zbtb20 estimated by quantitative RT-PCR (Q-PCR) was reduced by 90% in the SCN, 70% in the olfactory bulb and 90% in the cerebellum in NS-ZB20KO mice, with no change observed in Zbtb20 expression in the liver (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by Q-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Zbtb20 mRNA was reduced by 90% in the cerebellum of NS-ZB20KO mice.

evidence: The claim is supported by Q-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: No change was observed in Zbtb20 expression in the liver of NS-ZB20KO mice.

claim: ZBTB20 protein was abundantly expressed in the SCN neurons from WT mice.
source: Based on immunofluorescence staining, ZBTB20 protein was abundantly expressed in the SCN neurons from WT mice, but was almost undetectable in NS-ZB20KO mice determined by immunofluorescence staining (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: ZBTB20 protein was almost undetectable in NS-ZB20KO mice determined by immunofluorescence staining.
source: Based on immunofluorescence staining, ZBTB20 protein was abundantly expressed in the SCN neurons from WT mice, but was almost undetectable in NS-ZB20KO mice determined by immunofluorescence staining (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Expression of ZBTB20 was markedly reduced but not completely abolished in the hypothalami of NS-ZB20KO mice.
source: Western blot analysis using anti-ZBTB20 antibodies revealed that expression of ZBTB20 was markedly reduced but not completely abolished in the hypothalami of NS-ZB20KO mice, potentially due to non-Nestin-expressing cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: NS-ZB20KO mice were normal at birth.
source: NS-ZB20KO mice were normal at birth, but they began to display a range of abnormalities, including decreased body weight, body trembling, and hyperactivity after midnight (Video 1 and Video 2).
evidence: The claim is based on observations of NS-ZB20KO mice.

claim: NS-ZB20KO mice began to display abnormalities including decreased body weight, body trembling, and hyperactivity after midnight.
source: NS-ZB20KO mice were normal at birth, but they began to display a range of abnormalities, including decreased body weight, body trembling, and hyperactivity after midnight (Video 1 and Video 2).
evidence: The claim is based on observations of NS-ZB20KO mice shown in Videos 1 and 2.

claim: A significant proportion of NS-ZB20KO mice died at approximately 3–4 months.
source: A significant proportion of NS-ZB20KO mice died at approximately 3–4 months.
evidence: The claim is based on observations of NS-ZB20KO mice.

claim: Autopsy revealed reduced brain size and weight in NS-ZB20KO mice compared to Nestin-Cre transgenic mice or wild-type littermates.
source: Except for reduced brain size and weight, autopsy failed to reveal obvious alterations except for reduced brain size and weight in NS-ZB20KO mice compared to those in Nestin-Cre transgenic mice or wild-type littermates.
evidence: The claim is based on autopsy findings of NS-ZB20KO mice.

claim: Control mice exhibited normal bouts of restricted activity during the dark phase under LD cycles.

claim: Control mice exhibited normal free-running periods under DD conditions.

claim: NS-ZB20KO mice displayed a dramatic loss of the early evening activity under both LD and DD conditions.

claim: NS-ZB20KO mice displayed significantly limited durations in the early morning activity.

claim: Control mice displayed conspicuous evening activity and morning activity under LD cycles.

claim: NS-ZB20KO mice showed obviously reduced evening activity under LD cycles (CLAMS: n = 8, p=0.0078; DSI: n = 9, p=5.1E-07).

claim: NS-ZB20KO mice showed hyperactivity during the morning phase.

claim: ZBTB20 is essential for the sustained generation of evening activity rhythms.

claim: The phase-delaying effects caused by applying saturating light pulses at CT12-CT18 were significantly smaller in NS-ZB20KO mice than in control mice (WT: −3.18 ± 0.48 hr n = 6; NS-ZB20KO; −2.31 ± 0.36 hr n = 10).

claim: In response to a 6 hr phase advance of the LD cycle, the activity offset in NS-ZB20KO mice readjusted to the new LD regimen much more slowly than that in the control mice.

claim: In response to 6 hr phase-delay of the LD cycle, NS-ZB20KO mice ended their activity significantly earlier on day 1.

claim: There were no significant difference in the phase delay for the subsequent days between genotypes.

claim: Loss of Zbtb20 shapes the behavioral response to light perturbation.

claim: Relatively high enrichment of ZBTB20 binding occurred in the M2 region, which is 700 bp upstream of the transcriptional start site.

claim: The M1 site, located at 4.7 kb upstream from the TSS, showed a slight but significant signal for ZBTB20 binding.

claim: Acetylation of histone H3K9 occurred at the M2 site in the Prokr2 promoter.

claim: The rhythms originate from a central circadian pacemaker located in the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) of the hypothalamus.
source: The rhythms originate from a central circadian pacemaker located in the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) of the hypothalamus, and are synchronized to the environmental light-dark cycle via the retinohypothalamic tract (Morin and Allen, 2006; Reppert and Weaver, 2002; Vansteensel et al., 2008).

evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study (Mohawk et al., 2012).

evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study (Antle and Silver, 2005).
